content_html:
With an interest-only mortgage you pay only the interest for an agreed number of years, so the balance does not go down unless you choose to pay extra. When that period ends, the full balance must be repaid over the years left on the loan, and the payment rises, often sharply. This calculator shows both payments, the size of the jump and the total cost compared with a standard loan that repays principal from the start.

How to use this calculator

  1. Loan amount, interest rate and term: the amount borrowed, the annual rate and the full length of the loan, including the interest-only years.
  2. Interest-only period: how many years you pay interest only. Ten years is a common choice; it must be shorter than the term.
  3. More options: an optional extra principal payment during the interest-only years, and the rate a standard loan would charge, for the comparison.

How the payments are calculated

During the interest-only period the monthly payment is the balance times the annual rate divided by 12. With no extra payments the balance stays the same, so the payment does too.

When the period ends, the remaining balance is spread over the months left using the standard amortization formula, M = B × i ÷ (1 − (1 + i)−n), where i is the monthly rate and n the remaining number of months. Because the whole balance has to be repaid in fewer years, this payment is higher than a standard loan's payment over the full term.

Worked example

A $300,000 loan at 6.5% for 30 years with a 10-year interest-only period:

ItemInterest-only loanStandard loan
Payment, years 1 to 10$1,625.00$1,896.20
Payment, years 11 to 30$2,236.72$1,896.20
Balance after 10 years$300,000.00$254,328.38
Total interest$431,812.66$382,633.47

The payment rises by $611.72 a month, or 38%, in year 11, and the interest-only loan costs $49,179.19 more in interest. Paying an extra $200 a month during the first 10 years would cut the balance to $276,000 and the later payment to $2,057.78.

Who uses interest-only loans, and the risks

  • They can suit borrowers with irregular income who plan to pay down principal in lump sums, or buyers who expect to sell before principal repayments start.
  • You build no equity from payments during the interest-only years. If home prices fall, you could owe more than the home is worth.
  • The higher later payment has to fit your budget. Plan for it from day one rather than counting on refinancing.
  • Many interest-only loans also have adjustable rates. If yours does, check how the rate can change as well.

faq.question: Does an interest-only payment reduce what I owe?
faq.answer: No. An interest-only payment covers only the interest charged that month, so the balance stays the same unless you pay extra toward principal.

faq.question: Why is the payment after the interest-only period higher than a normal mortgage payment?
faq.answer: The full balance has to be repaid over fewer years. For example, after 10 interest-only years on a 30-year loan, the whole amount is repaid over the remaining 20 years.

faq.question: Can I make principal payments during the interest-only period?
faq.answer: Most interest-only loans allow it. Use the extra principal option to see how prepaying lowers the later payment and the total interest.

faq.question: Are interest-only mortgages easy to get?
faq.answer: They are less common than standard mortgages and lenders usually ask for strong credit, a larger down payment and proof you can afford the higher later payment.

faq.question: Does this include property tax and insurance?
faq.answer: No. The figures show principal and interest only. Add property tax, homeowners insurance and any HOA dues for your full monthly housing cost.
